doc.title: Vince DiMartino interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 8, 2025

title: Freddie's jazz bar and deciding against medicine
summary: He played at Freddie's American Jazz Bar with his exchange friends fed, then told his mother he would not be a doctor.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: “Oh boy you sound great.” And I said, “Well,” I said, “I’d like to play somewhere.” And they said, “Well there’s a place, it’s not in the best section of Bogota but it’s called ‘Freddie’s American Jazz Bar’ and they have a trio there that you might like to listen to at least.” And I said, “Well that’s great.” So I found my way over there, and I didn’t, you know this was great because you know the families you were staying with, they didn’t want you going to like, almost like going to Harlem or something. You know what I mean? They didn’t want you going there. They had glass in their wall around their house because you know crime is a big thing. They didn’t have a regular police force there. Military police. They carry machine guns. You know they walk around the city, you see these guys with machine guns you know. At night you hear [scats]. Sometimes you know I’m going I’m glad my mom and dad didn’t know about this you know what I mean because I didn’t know either. So anyway so I found this place and I went over there. Same kind of thing. They said, “Well you could bring your trumpet and we’d see what you do.” And I played a couple of tunes with them and they said, “Can you come back every week?” I said, “Well you know I have a lot of friends and we only can get together, I can only go out at night when I go out with my friends.” So if you will feed my friends — and you know it was a bar like, you know it was like a nice place but it was a bar. And he said, “Well we usually don’t have a lot of young people in here.” And I was about 18, 17. And I said, “Well can’t you make a place where they just sit?” “Okay.” And every time we’d come, almost every week and I’d come there and the table would be filled with food and I’d play and all my exchange student friends were there and they loved it and the people started coming you know. And so I said, “You know I really like doing this. This is what I really like to do” I said. And putting the thing in somebody’s mouth and seeing blood fly around with pieces of their teeth, that just really, I don’t think — what’s the choice here you know? So I had already, when I went back I talked to my mom first, I said, “Mom you know I don’t think I want to be a doctor.” And she said, “Well that’s all right.” I said, “Really?” She said, “Well you know look at you’re a really good student, look at what you’ve done on trumpet, look what you’ve done in school, why would I be worried about what you’re going to do? You’re going to do well.” You know and she was great. I said, “Wow, thanks for that, Mom, you can tell dad.” You know it was really funny. And my mom was really the center of our whole family, even the grandparents and everything. Because she had the joie de vivre. And when she said, “Oh come on we have to get together on Sunday, come on out from the city (my grandparents).”
What was that descriptor you just used for her?
Joy for life. © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-
